text: This question is for Dan Mlen.
>> All right, Brett, let's see it.
>> I was wondering if you could tell me
more about heroic Eve and the strands in
Judaism and Christianity that support
the idea that Eve was leaving innocence
for more knowledge and becoming more
like God, which was a positive thing. I
know there are some Jewish mystical and
philosophical strands, especially in
Kabala, that reframe the tree of
knowledge as a necessary step in kind of
our spiritual evolution. But what I
don't know is like how pervasive were
these theories and how heretical were
they considered by contemporaries in
their time. The context for this
question is that I'm turning 40 and I
went to get a tattoo consultation and I
was explaining this tattoo that I've
wanted because I I' love this idea of
reclaiming Eve and the guy who um was
wanting to do my tattoo said that he
wouldn't do it because it would be
celebrating sin. And I tried to explain
that, you know, the Gnostic texts look
at Eve differently or, you know,
Christian mystics and Jewish mystics,
but I wasn't really able to express, you
know, how heretical that view was
considered. Um, I don't really have a
sense for that. So, I wondered if you
could answer that question. And as
always, congrats on the book and keep up
the good work.
>> Hey, thank you for a great question,
Britt. Uh, I'm sorry you had to go
through an experience like that with a
tattoo artist. Uh, somebody engaged in a
profession that I think the majority of
Christians for the majority of the
history of Christianity would have
considered sinful, which has really only
been overcome within the last few
generations as tattoos have become more
popular, more secular, less
controversial, and Christians have
renegotiated their relationship with
tattoos and what the Bible says about
that. Uh, I got my tattoo when I was 19
in Deep Ellum in Dallas. It's a little
tribal design that I drew that's in
between my shoulder blades. And there
certainly wouldn't have been anyone in
that tattoo shop that would have had any
issue at all with an Eve tattoo. But to
address your question, I think you've
mentioned the two main groups in the
ancient and medieval and preodern world
that would have endorsed something like
a heroic Eve concept. Obviously, there's
a spectrum of ways this can be
understood all the way from Eve did
something wrong, but it was a result of
curiosity or something like that all the
way up to Eve was inspired by divine
wisdom and this was a way to liberate
humanity from uh the demi urge. So,
within Christianity, the Gnostic
literature is the main place where
you're going to find a heroic Eve. And
it again has different shapes and
different contours and things like that
depending on the text depending on if
it's Sethian or Valentinian or anything
like that. And obviously the Gnostic
literature was very popular with more
mystical strands of Christian thought up
until the fourth and fifth centuries
when it became demonized and
marginalized by the central church
institution. And this is the pattern
that you're going to find to the degree
a tradition has a centralized hierarchy.
The notion of a heroic Eve is probably
going to conflict with the rhetorical
goals and the structuring of power of
that hierarchy. That's certainly true
about Christianity once it arrogated
imperial power. I think to a lesser
degree that's true of Judaism. I think
mystical Judaism was able to survive and
spread more because Judaism didn't have
as much of a centralized authority
structure. uh but it still was probably
on the outs with the most influential
voices within Judaism in the medieval
and later periods. And then outside
ofnosticism and mystical Judaism, it
begins to bubble to the surface again
within the scholarship that begins uh
with Renaissance humanism and then
develops in the 19th and 20th centuries.
So you had some Renaissance scholars who
were arguing for a more egalitarian
uh approach to understanding the role of
women in the garden of Eden in the
scriptures. And then you have later
scholars within Jewish and Christian
traditions who are doing very similar
things. Phyllis Trible uh God and the
rhetoric of sexuality for instance is a
good discussion that tries to kind of
reclaim Eve. And then also Judith
Plascow's the coming of Lilith does a
very similar thing from a Jewish
perspective. And I think one of the main
problems with the traditions that have
that centralized authority structure is
the fact that that reading kind of
conflicts with the New Testament and
with other texts that are reflecting on
what's going on in the Garden of Eden.
You have 1 Timothy 2:14, I think it is,
where uh the person pretending to be
Paul says that it was not Adam who was
deceived, but the woman who was deceived
uh and became a transgressor as a
result. And that hierarchy is going to
give priority to the passages that
support its structuring of power, which
was very patriarchal by the fourth,
fifth centuries CE. And so the passage
that says that the women screwed up is
going to take priority over an
interpretation of the Garden of Eden
story that says, "Hey, maybe Eve was on
to something." Uh, but you will still
have around the periphery of a lot of
Christian and Jewish traditions today,
folks trying to reclaim something for
Eve. And I think there's something to
that as well within the story of the
Garden of Eden. I think if we never had
any other biblical texts, if we just had
Genesis 2 and 3, we would probably
understand
God to be a bit of an antagonist, a
villain who is trying to stop humanity
from progressing. And it's natural for
humans to want to overcome their
shortcomings, want to overcome their
limits. And I think we would need to
sympathize. And also, as I have talked
about on my channel many times, uh the
serpent is not really lying in the story
of the Garden of Eden. If anyone is
lying, it would have to be God who
threatens Adam with death on the very
day he eats from the tree of the
knowledge of good and evil. And then
Adam doesn't die on that very day. So I
think the traditional dichotomy of good
and evil and what's going on in the
Garden of Eden has always been
contextualized and negotiated through
the interpretive lenses of later
understandings of the significance of
this event later treatments of this
notion of a fall which is common to
Christianity but not really common to
Judaism and you know Paul's
representation of Eve as the woman who
was deceived at least in the pseudo
Pauline text. So there's a lot going on
there. Uh I think it probably was
considered pretty heretical by the folks
who were in positions of power within
Christianity particularly but also
within Judaism but it is something that
has come to the four in the last few
centuries as a result of attempts to
renegotiate what's going on in the text
to interpret the text through more
egalitarian perspectives that don't try
to demonize or vilify a human for doing
what humans do. though I would say that
tattoo artist is taking their tradition
more seriously than they are taking the
text of the Bible. But that's also
probably why they don't have a problem
with being a tattoo artist. And I think
that's a good thing. But in that
negotiation, I think people need to take
more seriously the question of whose
interests are being elevated, whose
interests are being marginalized or
ignored. And if they think critically
about that, I think they're going to see
there's a lot more harm that results
from that kind of maintenance of those
power structures than there is good. And
that in and of itself would kind of be
celebrating sin in a way. So, thank you
for a wonderful question. I hope that
was somewhat helpful. I don't know that
I provided any information that you
didn't already have. Uh, but that's my
thoughts on the matter. And the fit for
this video has been the Avengers.
